strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: accelerating Diffusion Policy inference for real-time robot control, an underexplored application of diffusion caching techniques.

The method is well-motivated by clear empirical observations (non-uniform temporal and block-wise feature similarity patterns), and the error surge phenomenon is analyzed both theoretically (Proposition 3.1 with a complete proof) and experimentally (correlation and controlled-input experiments).

The Adaptive Caching Scheduler is a clean formulation: cache schedule selection is cast as a dynamic programming problem, giving an optimal solution under the similarity objective with negligible overhead, enabled by a justified episode-homogeneity assumption that is supported with dedicated evidence (Appendix A.10, A.15).

Extensive and convincing evaluation: simulation benchmarks (RoboMimic PH/MH, Push-T, Block Pushing, Kitchen), a VLA model (RDT-1B on ManiSkill), a real-robot Franka deployment with latency/frequency measurements, and ablations isolating ACS and BUA contributions.

Thorough supplementary material: hyperparameter sensitivity (n, S), similarity metric ablations, update-step tables, cache behavior visualizations, integration with DDIM, and a stated plan to release code, supporting reproducibility.
The BUA ablation result (block-wise scheduling alone performs worse than unified, then recovers with BUA) compellingly validates the paper's central failure-mode claim.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method is a fairly natural combination of existing ideas (feature caching, adaptive timestep selection as in TeaCache/FORA, and per-block scheduling), applied to a new domain. The individual components are incremental relative to prior diffusion caching literature.

The DP objective (maximizing summed cosine similarities) is a heuristic proxy; no theoretical or empirical link is established between this objective and end-task success rate, so the scheduler's 'optimality' is only with respect to a surrogate.

The 'lossless' claim is overstated: at the more aggressive settings (S=7), performance degrades noticeably on some tasks (e.g., Can_mh 0.39/0.79, Transport_mh 0.17 avg in Table 1), and the appendix admits performance collapse at small S. BAC is lossless only relative to full precision at S=10 on most, not all, settings.

Advantages over the Uniform baseline are not uniform: at comparable FLOPs, Uniform(fast) matches or exceeds BAC's average success rate in the PH benchmark (0.79 vs 0.74), so BAC's benefit concentrates on specific hard tasks (Kitchen, Tool Hang), which weakens the generality of the claimed gains.
Two tuned hyperparameters (n and S) with demonstrated strong interplay (Table 3) create a nontrivial per-task tuning burden, partly undermining the 'training-free plug-and-play for free' framing.
Real-world evaluation covers only a single custom task with a single setup; breadth of real-world evidence is limited compared to the simulation results.

The baseline set is narrow: comparisons are mainly against uniform caching and an adapted TeaCache; no comparison with other acceleration approaches for policies (e.g., distillation, action-chunk reduction, other DiT caching methods like Delta-DiT adapted to this setting), and the l1-norm error-score heuristic for Stage 1 of BUA is justified only by intuition.

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('dertermine', 'Notebly', 'Pusht-T'), a marginal notation slip in the LayerNorm error derivation (Eq. 23 mixing δ_ij and δ_j), and the 'Placeholder Publisher' / template artifacts in references suggest the paper was not fully polished.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: real-time control with diffusion-based policies is genuinely latency-bound, and a training-free acceleration plugin is a useful contribution to the robotics/systems community.

The 'error surge' analysis is the most interesting part of the paper. The authors provide both a first-order theoretical analysis (Proposition 3.1, showing how upstream errors propagate through LayerNorm-FFN blocks) and well-designed toy experiments (controlled scaling factor, Pearson correlation of r=0.99) to isolate inter-block error propagation. The finding that block-wise caching can perform *worse* than unified caching is non-obvious and empirically substantiated in the ablation (Fig. 7b).

The evaluation is broad: RoboMimic (PH/MH), Push-T, Block Pushing, Kitchen, RDT-1B on ManiSkill, plus a real-robot deployment with latency measurements, ablations over hyperparameters (n, S), similarity metrics (MSE/L1/Wasserstein/cosine), and integration with DDIM schedulers (Appendix A.16).

The appendix provides substantial supporting evidence, including the episode-homogeneity analysis (Appendix A.15) that justifies computing the schedule once per task, and detailed per-task cache schedules for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core mechanism — reusing block outputs when consecutive-step feature similarity is high — is a close variant of existing caching heuristics (TeaCache, FORA, δ-DiT, token-wise caching). The Adaptive Caching Scheduler is essentially interval selection maximizing summed cosine similarity, solvable by standard DP; the 'optimal' framing overstates what is a similarity heuristic (cosine similarity of intermediate features is a weak proxy for downstream action quality, and no analysis links maximizing it to policy success). Block-level caching schedules also already exist in 'Cache Me If You Can' (Wimbauer et al., 2024), which the related-work section dismisses as U-Net-specific without sufficient justification. The BUA is a fairly ad-hoc heuristic (top-n selection plus union of update sets).

The 'lossless' claim is stronger than the evidence. Table 1 shows BAC(S=7) degrades severely on MH data (e.g., Can 0.39 vs. 0.92 full precision; AVG 0.60 vs. 0.76), and even at S=10 Transport_mh drops below full precision. Appendix A.16 shows large collapses at S=3 and S=5 on several MH tasks. The method is highly sensitive to S and n (Tool_hang collapses from 0.49 to 0.03 when n goes from 5 to 3), which undercuts the 'for free' framing — in practice the hyperparameters must be tuned per setting, and the paper offers no principled way to choose them.

Weak baseline coverage. Only two cache baselines (Uniform and an adapted TeaCache) are compared against. Given the paper's positioning, comparisons with token-wise caching (ToCa), FORA, Learning-to-Cache, or DDIM/DPM-Solver step-reduction at matched FLOPs are needed to establish that the added complexity of per-block scheduling is worthwhile.

Concerns about internal consistency and setup. The BUA-added step lists (Tables 17–28) add dozens of update steps to early blocks (e.g., 36 added steps for layers.0.FFN on Can_ph), which seems in tension with the reported FLOPs savings; the FLOPs accounting is not clearly explained. In the real-world experiments, DDPM K=100 achieving only 3% success while BAC S=5 achieves 63% is surprising and the custom single-task hardware setup is under-specified, making these numbers hard to contextualize. The offline cost of collecting similarity matrices (requiring full-precision rollouts across K timesteps) is claimed to be 'virtually no additional cost' but is never quantified.

Presentation and rigor issues. The reference list contains many malformed/placeholder entries ('Placeholder Publisher', 'Submitted to Some Conference, unpublished'), and there are numerous typos ('dertermine', 'Pusht-T', 'Notebly', 'paradigams'). Proposition 3.1 is a routine first-order Taylor expansion through LayerNorm; presenting it as theoretical depth overstates its contribution. The theory also relies on assumptions (bounded second derivative, σ(X) ≥ σmin) whose validity for trained Diffusion Policy checkpoints is not verified.

Significance is narrower than claimed. The method only applies to transformer-based Diffusion Policies and relies on the episode-homogeneity property of relatively narrow manipulation tasks (evidenced mainly on RoboMimic-style benchmarks); how it transfers to highly diverse, open-ended settings is unaddressed, and the authors' own limitation (amplifying error when the base policy is weak) is significant for real deployments.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: accelerating Diffusion Policy for real-time robot control, an area that existing caching work (DeepCache, TeaCache, FORA, etc.) does not directly cover, with a clear motivation (10 Hz vs. required 30-50 Hz).

The Adaptive Caching Scheduler is well-motivated: the observation of non-uniform, block-specific temporal similarity (Fig. 1) is convincingly documented, and reformulating update-step selection as a dynamic programming problem over interval similarities is a clean and efficient solution.

The 'error surge' analysis is a nice contribution: the paper identifies and formalizes inter-block caching error propagation through FFN blocks (Proposition 3.1 with a first-order perturbation analysis plus proof in Appendix A.4), and supports it with controlled toy experiments (Pearson r=0.9894, scaling-factor study) and consistent visualizations (Figs. 14-15).

Comprehensive evaluation: real-world Franka deployment with latency/frequency measurements, RoboMimic PH/MH, Push-T, Block Pushing, Kitchen, and generalization to the RDT-1B VLA model on ManiSkill; results are averaged over multiple checkpoints and 3 seeds, with success rate, FLOPs, and wall-clock speedup all reported.

Thorough ablations (Unified ACS vs. Block-wise ACS vs. +BUA), hyperparameter sensitivity for n and S, comparison across similarity metrics (MSE/L1/Wasserstein/cosine), and evidence that BAC stacks with DDIM (Appendix A.16), showing gains are not merely from step reduction.

The episode-homogeneity analysis (Appendix A.10, A.15) provides both qualitative and quantitative justification for the one-off offline scheduler computation, and credibly distinguishes action generation from image generation tasks.
Reproducibility statement is detailed; benchmarks are public, hyperparameters are disclosed, and code release is promised.
weaknesses: Per-task offline calibration is a significant practical caveat: ACS requires full-precision rollouts to compute similarity matrices, and BUA's error scores (Eq. 13) require all-pairs feature comparisons. The 'virtually no additional cost' claim relies on episode homogeneity, which is strong in simulation but less certain for the real-world task or when task/scene distributions shift; robustness to distribution shift is not evaluated.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters undermines the plug-and-play framing: performance varies substantially with n and S (e.g., Tool_hang collapses from 0.49/0.55 at n=5 to 0.03/0.07 at n=3, Table 2; Kitchen p4 drops from 0.94/0.97 at S=10 to 0.23/0.39 at S=7, Table 1), and BUA can add many update steps (Table 17: layers.0.FFN gains ~36 of 100 steps), eroding speedup. No principled or automatic selection of n/S is provided.

The 'lossless'/'for free' claims are overstated in places: MH Transport and PH Tool_hang show noticeable drops vs. full precision (e.g., 0.30/0.46 vs. 0.35/0.46; 0.49/0.55 vs. 0.43/0.53 is actually a gain, but MH Transport is not), and the real-world task is a single task with modest trial counts (71% and 63% success rates reported without confidence intervals).

Baseline coverage is somewhat thin: the main comparison is a uniform-caching baseline and a ported TeaCache; no comparison to other training-free acceleration approaches (e.g., step-skipping/consistency distillation hybrids, token-level caching like ToCa directly, quantization, or DPMSolver variants beyond DDIM) at matched budgets.

Novelty is incremental relative to image/video-domain caching literature: block-level or layer-wise adaptive caching schedules have been explored (e.g., Learning-to-Cache, delta-DiT, hierarchical caching); the contribution is mostly adaptation to the robotics setting plus the DP formulation and BUA heuristic. BUA itself is a simple heuristic (top-k selection plus union of schedules) whose justification is largely empirical.

Some organizational/presentation issues: 'Project page:' in the abstract is blank, several references contain placeholder text ('Placeholder Publisher', 'Submitted to Some Conference, unpublished'), and Section 3.3's closing sentence and Fig. 4 interpretation could be tightened; the trend that BUA additions push layers.0.FFN toward near-uniform updates suggests the final schedule is close to a hybrid heuristic, which deserves more discussion.
The theoretical analysis (Proposition 3.1) is a first-order local approximation and does not directly predict which schedules fail; it motivates but does not quantitatively guide the BUA design.
